paras: The lynching of James Fowler took place at Custer City, Dakota Territory, early on February 7, 1881, when about twenty masked men took Fowler, known as "Fly Specked Billy," from Sheriff John T. Code and his deputies and hanged him from a pine tree. Fowler had been arrested a few hours earlier, accused of shooting dead Abe Barnes, a freighter, in a Custer City billiard hall. A Deadwood dispatch carried the story across the West and Midwest, and the local Custer Chronicle printed an approving account with testimony from both inquests.

Barnes, a freighter living at Kearney Junction, Nebraska, was hauling freight toward Custer when Fowler joined his train on the road about twenty miles below town. The Chronicle called Fowler "a desperate character, an outlaw," and inquest witnesses described him as a known horse thief. Arriving on Sunday, February 6, he spent the day threatening men in saloons with a revolver borrowed from Barnes.

About ten o'clock that night Fowler entered George Palmer's billiard hall, snapped the pistol at several men, and then seized Barnes by the shoulder and shot him. According to witness W. W. Summers, Fowler said "come up to the bar and take a drink" as he fired, and other witnesses knew of no trouble between the two men. Barnes died within minutes, and Fowler, clubbed with a pistol as he ran for the door, fell into the arms of Sheriff Code.

Code took his prisoner to Pat McHugh's saloon and bound him, because, he testified, there was no jail fit to hold him. Fearing "an attempt to lynch his man" amid public "indignation," Code waited until the crowd dispersed. About one o'clock, as Code, deputies Frank Peters and Wm. Quinn, and McHugh carried the bound prisoner to the sheriff's cabin, masked men sprang from concealment, pushed the officers inside at revolver point, and hauled Fowler away.
Code and the coroner followed the tracks to the edge of the timber across French creek, about a quarter of a mile south of the cabin, and found Fowler hanging dead from a pine tree.

Coroner Oliver C. Garthwait's jury viewed both bodies and found that Barnes had been shot by Fowler "with feionious [felonious] intent." At Fowler's inquest, physician D. W. Flick gave the cause of death as "asphyxia or strangulation," and the officers testified that they recognized none of the masked men. The printed verdict on Fowler is cut off in the surviving copy, and no report of arrests of the lynchers was found.

The first reports came from a Deadwood telegram of February 7, which said Barnes had declined Fowler's invitation to drink and that Fowler was "taken away by the vigilantes" and found hanging to a tree. Between February 8 and 17 the item ran in Cheyenne, Omaha, Sacramento, Helena, Yankton, Elko and Ohio, usually without comment, though Sacramento headed it "A Murderer at Custer City, D. T., Hanged by the Vigilantes."

The Custer Chronicle's headlines, "Death's Round-Up, by Revolver and Rope" and "A Murderer and Judge Lynch Become Acquainted," set the tone of its account. It called the shooting "a cold blooded and unprovoked murder," praised Barnes as "a highly respected man," and wrote that "Judge Lynch had executed his inexorable sentence cleverly and secretly." None of the papers mentioned the race of Fowler, Barnes or the lynchers.

A month later a brief credited to the Omaha Bee ran in Montana, once in the Helena Weekly Herald's joke column; it renamed the freighter "Burns" and said Fowler was "taken from the jail" by "an infuriated mob." By mid-March the case had become gossip, as papers reported that "Fly Specked Billy" was seen walking near the place where he was hanged.

The March brief's statement that Fowler was taken from a jail conflicts with the sworn testimony of the sheriff and a deputy that he was seized at the door of the sheriff's cabin because no fit jail existed. The wire's motive, that Barnes was shot for refusing a drink, is not borne out by the inquest witnesses, who described Fowler seizing Barnes and firing as he spoke the invitation.

accounts.gist: Barnes was asked to drink by Fowler, declined, and was shot dead; Fowler was taken away by the vigilantes and found next morning hanging to a tree.

accounts.label: Custer Chronicle and inquest testimony
accounts.gist: After a day of threatening men in saloons, Fowler seized Barnes in a billiard hall and shot him as he said 'come up to the bar and take a drink'; about twenty masked men took Fowler from the sheriff at his cabin door, there being no fit jail, and hanged him across French creek.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee brief (March)
accounts.gist: Fowler, angered that 'a freighter named Burns' refused to drink with him, shot him and was taken from the jail that night and lynched by an infuriated mob.

framing.detail: The Custer Chronicle headlined 'A Murderer and Judge Lynch Become Acquainted' and wrote that Fowler had 'paid the penalty' and his soul fled 'to the tortures of an eternity of punishment'.
The Deadwood dispatch ran without comment under heads such as 'A Black Hills Tragedy', 'Shot Dead.' and 'A Murderer at Custer City, D. T., Hanged by the Vigilantes.'
A month later the Omaha Bee brief ran in Montana among jokes and news notes, and Custer's 'ghost' became a gossip item.
